full_text_en:
Shinho Merchant Marine Co., Ltd. of South Korea v. Sichuan Ouyang General Trading Company, et al.
— Dispute over Jurisdiction Objection in Letter of Credit Fraud Case

Promulgated by the Supreme People's Court (2001) No. 35

Supreme People's Court of the People's Republic of China
Civil Ruling

Case No. (2000) Jing Zhong Zi No. 155

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Shinho Merchant Marine Co., Ltd. of South Korea. Domicile: 309-3 Galma-dong, Seo-gu, Daejeon Metropolitan City, South Korea.
Legal Representative: Lee Soon-ki, Representative Director.
Authorized Agent: Zhang Yaojun, Attorney at Beijing Lide Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Sichuan Ouyang General Trading Company. Domicile: 5th Floor, Fuzuan Building, No. 78 Section 2, Hongxing Road, Chengdu City, Sichuan Province, People's Republic of China.
Legal Representative: Huang Xinyu, Chairman of the Board.

Third Party at First Instance: National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (Nonghyup) of South Korea. Domicile: 75 Chungjeong-ro 1-gil, Jung-gu, Seoul, South Korea.
Legal Representative: Won Cheol-hee, President.

Third Party at First Instance: Chengdu Zongfu Sub-branch, Agricultural Bank of China.
Responsible Person: Pan Qiong, Deputy Branch Manager.

Shinho Merchant Marine Co., Ltd. of South Korea (hereinafter referred to as Shinho) appealed against the Civil Ruling (1999) Chuan Jing Chu Zi No. 1 of the Sichuan High People's Court concerning a jurisdiction objection in a dispute over letter of credit fraud with Sichuan Ouyang General Trading Company (hereinafter referred to as Ouyang), National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (hereinafter referred to as Nonghyup), and Chengdu Zongfu Sub-branch, Agricultural Bank of China (hereinafter referred to as Chengdu Zongfu Sub-branch, ABC). This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law, comprising Li Jian, Deputy Chief Judge of the Second Civil Division, as Presiding Judge, and Acting Judges Qian Xiaochen and Chen Jizhong as members, to conduct the trial.

During the second instance of this Court, the following facts relating to the jurisdiction of this case were ascertained: On December 4, 1998, Ouyang filed a lawsuit with the Sichuan High People's Court against Shinho as defendant, naming Nonghyup and the International Business Department of the Agricultural Bank of China, Sichuan Branch (hereinafter referred to as the International Business Department, ABC) as third parties. The claims were: 1. To declare invalid and terminate payment under the letters of credit opened and accepted by the issuing bank, the Agricultural Bank of China, Sichuan Branch, with the plaintiff as applicant and the defendant as beneficiary, payable to the negotiating bank, Nonghyup; 2. To order the defendant to bear all litigation costs of this case. The facts alleged were: Between September and October 1997, Ouyang and Shinho executed four sales contracts by facsimile in Chengdu, Sichuan, China, providing for payment by letters of credit. Accordingly, Ouyang, as applicant, applied to the issuing bank, the International Business Department, ABC, to open five letters of credit between April and August 1997, with Shinho as beneficiary and Nonghyup as negotiating bank. The total amount of the letters of credit opened and accepted was USD 9,867,601.93. However, Shinho neither supplied the goods nor shipped them, and deliberately created false shipping documents for the purpose of fraud. The ship designated by Shinho for carriage was to arrive at the destination port of Shantou no later than the end of October 1997, but the Shantou Maritime Safety Administration of the Ministry of Communications of the People's Republic of China certified that between January and December 1997, no such vessel "had completed entry and exit formalities at our office." After Ouyang discovered this, it promptly notified Shinho, but Shinho never responded. Meanwhile, Nonghyup, as the negotiating bank, knowing that the documents submitted by the defendant beneficiary were false, submitted these false documents to the issuing bank, the International Business Department, ABC, thereby fraudulently obtaining acceptance of the amounts under the four letters of credit. The negotiating bank, Nonghyup, colluded with the beneficiary, Shinho, deliberately concealing the falsity of the documents, and its conduct completely violated the principles of good faith, credit, and honesty, thus constituting fraud.

Before filing the lawsuit, on November 6, 1998, Ouyang applied to the Sichuan High People's Court for an order to stop payment under the letters of credit, naming Shinho as the respondent and the International Business Department, ABC as the third party. On November 18, 1998, the Sichuan High People's Court issued a Civil Ruling (1998) Chuan Li Bao Zi No. 9, freezing the amounts totaling USD 9,867,591.83 under the ABC International Business Department's letters of credit Nos. 220LC9706124, 220LC9704079, 220LC9709161, and 220LC9709162. Nonghyup submitted a defense on the merits, while Shinho raised a jurisdiction objection based on an arbitration clause contained in the sales contract between it and Ouyang. The arbitration clause stipulated: "All disputes arising between the parties shall be finally settled by a commercial arbitration commission of a third country in accordance with commercial arbitration rules."

The Sichuan High People's Court held that: The arbitration clause relied upon by Shinho in raising the jurisdiction objection was an agreement between Shinho and Ouyang in the sales contract and was unrelated to the letter of credit fraud dispute in this case. Moreover, the clause stated: "Arbitration: All disputes arising between the parties shall be finally settled by a commercial arbitration commission of a third country in accordance with commercial arbitration rules." This clause was unclear, and Ouyang's choice to file a lawsuit in court indicated that it had waived its right to renegotiate and clarify the clause. Pursuant to Article 18 of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China, this arbitration clause was invalid. In accordance with Article 38 and Article 249 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling was as follows: The jurisdiction objection raised by Shinho Merchant Marine Co., Ltd. of South Korea was dismissed. Shinho, dissatisfied with the original ruling, appealed to this Court, arguing: 1. The original ruling's finding that "the arbitration clause relied upon by Shinho in raising the jurisdiction objection was an agreement between Shinho and Ouyang in the sales contract and was unrelated to the letter of credit fraud dispute in this case" was erroneous. If this case involved letter of credit fraud and the appellant was the perpetrator, the victim would be the negotiating bank, Nonghyup, or the issuing bank, Chengdu Zongfu Sub-branch, ABC, not Ouyang. The plaintiff in this case should be Nonghyup or Chengdu Zongfu Sub-branch, ABC, not Ouyang. 2. The original ruling's determination that the arbitration clause agreed upon between Shinho and Ouyang in the contract was "unclear, and Ouyang's choice to file a lawsuit in court indicated that it had waived its right to renegotiate and clarify the clause," and therefore the arbitration clause was invalid, was also erroneous. Renegotiating the arbitration clause was both a right and an obligation of Ouyang. Rights may be waived, but obligations must be performed. Ouyang's unilateral action violated the provisions of Chinese law and could not lead to the conclusion that "the arbitration clause is invalid." 3. The original ruling's application of Article 18 of the Arbitration Law of the People's Republic of China to dismiss the appellant's jurisdiction objection was also erroneous. In this case, Ouyang had not discussed with the appellant the matter of entering into a supplementary agreement, let alone the fact that a supplementary agreement could not be reached. Therefore, the original ruling's application of Article 18 of the Arbitration Law to dismiss the appellant's jurisdiction objection was an error in the application of law. Shinho requested the court of second instance to render a fair ruling in accordance with the law.

The appellee, Ouyang, did not submit a defense.

This Court holds: The claim filed by the plaintiff at first instance, Ouyang, in the court of first instance was to declare the letters of credit invalid. The defendant in the lawsuit was the beneficiary of the letters of credit—the seller under the underlying sales contract, Shinho. The cause of action was fraud in the underlying transaction. Since the most direct legal relationship between the two parties is the sales contract, and the letters of credit are the payment mechanism agreed upon in that contract, Ouyang is the applicant, and Shinho is the beneficiary of the letters of credit. Ouyang's basis for suing Shinho for letter of credit fraud is the allegation that Shinho used forged documents in an attempt to fraudulently obtain the proceeds under the letters of credit. The ruling of the court of first instance, which stated that it was only adjudicating the letter of credit relationship, was inappropriate as it deviated from the basis of Ouyang's lawsuit. The arbitration clause in the sales contract between Shinho and Ouyang is an unclear and unenforceable arbitration clause that requires renegotiation by the parties. However, Ouyang has already chosen litigation to resolve the dispute in this case, indicating that it has abandoned its willingness to arbitrate. Shinho's assertion that renegotiation is both a right and an obligation of the parties lacks factual and legal basis. The determination of the court of first instance on this point is correct. Pursuant to Article 145 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China: "In accordance with Article 111(2) of the Civil Procedure Law, if the parties have stipulated an arbitration clause in a written contract, or have reached a written arbitration agreement after a dispute arises, and one party files a lawsuit with a people's court, the people's court shall rule that the case is not accepted and shall inform the plaintiff to apply for arbitration to an arbitration institution. However, this does not apply if the arbitration clause or arbitration agreement is invalid, has become ineffective, or its content is unclear and cannot be enforced." Since the arbitration clause in the original sales contract did not specify the method and institution of arbitration, its content was unclear and unenforceable. Therefore, the court of first instance should accept Ouyang's lawsuit.

Although a letter of credit is a method of settlement within an underlying transaction, it is independent of the underlying transaction and is a documentary transaction governed by the principle of strict compliance. Under normal circumstances, a party may not request the suspension of payment or the invalidation of a letter of credit based on matters arising from the underlying transaction. An exception to this principle is the letter of credit fraud exception principle. The so-called "letter of credit fraud exception principle" means that when there is material fraud in the underlying transaction, it may constitute an exception to the independence of the letter of credit relationship from the underlying transaction. Since the application of the "fraud exception principle" is premised on fraud in the underlying transaction, and leads to the consequence of stopping payment under the letter of credit, it is necessary to adjudicate the underlying transaction dispute together with the legal relationship of the letter of credit. Since China's Civil Procedure Law provides for a third-party system, and the plaintiff at first instance, Ouyang's claims include requests regarding the validity of the letters of credit and the termination of payment, if Ouyang prevails and its request for suspension of payment under the letters of credit is granted, the result will necessarily involve whether the negotiating bank's claim for the issuing bank to perform its obligations under the letters of credit is established. If Ouyang loses, the issuing bank will be liable for payment under the letters of credit. It can be considered that the outcome of this case is legally related to the interests of the issuing bank and the negotiating bank. Therefore, the court of first instance did not err in naming Chengdu Zongfu Sub-branch, ABC, and Nonghyup as third parties in this case. However, precisely because the trial of this case involves both the underlying relationship—the sales contract—and the letter of credit dispute, the cause of action of this case should be determined as a dispute over payment by letter of credit in an international sale of goods. In summary, the court of first instance has jurisdiction over both the sales contract dispute and the letter of credit dispute, and its ruling dismissing Shinho's objection is correct. Therefore, in accordance with Article 24 and Article 38 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court rules as follows:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original ruling is affirmed.

The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 50 yuan shall be borne by Shinho Merchant Marine Co., Ltd. of South Korea.

This ruling is final.

Presiding Judge: Li Jian
Acting Judge: Qian Xiaochen
Acting Judge: Chen Jizhong

Dated: December 13, 2000

Clerk: Gao Xiaoli
